    Chapter 13

    Certificates and PKI: The Internet's ID Cards

    🤔 Anyone can generate a key and claim to be your bank. So who vouches that this key really belongs to bank.com?

    • ⏱️ ~14 min
    • 📚 16 sections
    • 🎮 3 interactive
    • ⭐ 255 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    13.1The problem certificates solve#

    Chapter 10 ended with a warning: key exchange alone can't stop Mallory in the middle. When your browser receives a public key that claims to belong to bank.example, how does it know the key isn't Mallory's?

    You can't meet every website's owner to swap keys in person. You need someone you already trust to vouch for the key.

    ✔ section read

    13.2The passport analogy#

    Think of how passports work:

    1. You prove your identity to a passport office (a trusted authority).
    2. The office issues a document binding your name to your photo, protected by anti-forgery features.
    3. A border officer in another country has never met you, but trusts the passport office, checks the document is genuine and unexpired, and checks that the photo matches your face.

    A digital certificate does exactly this for public keys:

    Passport Certificate
    Your name The website's domain name (bank.example)
    Your photo The website's public key
    Passport office Certificate Authority (CA)
    Holograms and special paper The CA's digital signature
    Expiry date Validity dates
    Border officer Your browser
    "Does the photo match your face?" "Does the server prove it holds the private key matching the certificate's public key?"

    That last row is important. Certificates are public. Anyone can download Google's certificate. Mallory can copy it, but it's useless to her without Google's private key. During the TLS handshake, the server must sign something with that private key to prove the certificate is really its own (Chapter 14).

    A Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the whole system around certificates: the authorities, the rules, the software and the processes for issuing, checking and revoking them.

    ✔ section read

    13.3What's inside a certificate#

    The standard format is called X.509 (version 3). Here's a real certificate, created in the lab at the end of this chapter, printed by OpenSSL with notes added:

    The most important fields:

    Field Meaning
    Subject Who the certificate identifies. CN = Common Name, O = Organization, C = Country.
    Subject Alternative Name (SAN) The domain names (and/or IP addresses) the certificate is valid for. Browsers only check this field, not the Common Name.
    Issuer The CA that signed it
    Validity Not Before / Not After dates
    Public key The key being vouched for
    Serial number Unique per CA; used for revocation
    Basic Constraints CA:TRUE means it can sign other certificates; CA:FALSE means it's an end certificate
    Key Usage / Extended Key Usage What the key may be used for: server authentication, client authentication, code signing, email, signing certificates
    CRL Distribution Points / Authority Information Access Where to check revocation and download the issuer's certificate
    Signed Certificate Timestamps (SCTs) Proof the certificate was published in Certificate Transparency logs (section 13.11)
    Signature The CA's signature over all of the above
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    13.4Certificate authorities and the chain of trust#

    A Certificate Authority (CA) is an organization trusted to verify identities and sign certificates. Examples include Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, Sectigo, GlobalSign and Google Trust Services.

    CAs are organized in a hierarchy:

    (The names above are the actual chain example.com served when this guide was written; it included one more intermediate between the two shown.)

    • Root CA: the anchor of trust. Its certificate is self-signed (it vouches for itself) and comes pre-installed in your device's trust store. Root private keys are kept offline in hardware security modules inside guarded facilities, and used only in formal, recorded "key ceremonies" with multiple witnesses.
    • Intermediate CA: signed by the root and used for daily issuing. This keeps the root key offline and safe. If an intermediate is compromised, only it has to be replaced.
    • Leaf certificate: the server's own certificate.

    Trust stores. Your device trusts a list of roots (roughly 100–150) maintained by the operating system or browser vendor: Apple, Microsoft, Google (the Chrome Root Store), and Mozilla (also used by many Linux systems). To be included, CAs must follow strict rules (the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements) and pass regular independent audits. CAs that break the rules get removed (section 13.14).

    The server sends its leaf certificate plus the intermediates. The browser already has the root. If a server forgets to send an intermediate, some clients will fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate." It's one of the most common setup mistakes.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    13.5How your browser checks a certificate#

    When you connect to https://bank.example, your browser, in a few milliseconds:

    1. Builds the chain: leaf → intermediate(s) → a root in its trust store.
    2. Verifies every signature in the chain: the root signed the intermediate, the intermediate signed the leaf.
    3. Checks the dates on every certificate. (This is why a computer with a wrong clock shows certificate errors everywhere.)
    4. Checks the name: bank.example must appear in the leaf's Subject Alternative Name.
    5. Checks the rules: intermediates must have CA:TRUE; the leaf must be allowed for "TLS Web Server Authentication."
    6. Checks revocation (has this certificate been cancelled?), using whatever method the browser supports.
    7. Checks Certificate Transparency: major browsers require proof the certificate was publicly logged.
    8. Checks possession: during the TLS handshake, the server signs the handshake data with the private key that matches the certificate. Without the private key, a copied certificate is worthless.

    If any step fails, you get a warning page.

    ✔ section read

    13.6How a certificate is created#

    How does a CA check that you control a domain? The automated methods (defined by a protocol called ACME, used by Let's Encrypt and others) are:

    Method What you do Good for
    HTTP-01 Serve a specific token at http://yourdomain/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token> Ordinary web servers
    DNS-01 Create a DNS TXT record _acme-challenge.yourdomain containing a token Wildcard certificates; servers not reachable from the internet
    TLS-ALPN-01 Answer a special TLS handshake on port 443 Setups where only port 443 is open
    ✔ section read

    13.7Validation levels: DV, OV and EV#

    Level What the CA verifies Cost and speed What you see in the browser
    DV (Domain Validation) Only that the requester controls the domain Free to cheap; automatic, in seconds Padlock
    OV (Organization Validation) Domain + that the organization legally exists Paid; days Padlock (organization visible in certificate details)
    EV (Extended Validation) Domain + organization with stricter checks Expensive; days to weeks Padlock. (Browsers removed the green "company name" bar around 2019, after research showed users didn't notice it and it could be gamed.)

    The vast majority of the web uses DV certificates.

    ⚠️ Watch out: the padlock does NOT mean a site is trustworthy. It means your connection is encrypted and that you're connected to the domain shown in the address bar. Phishing sites get free DV certificates too. paypa1-secure-login.example can have a perfectly valid padlock. Always check the domain name.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Certificate validation levels

    ✅ Use it
    DV

    Domain Validation

    • Free and automatic (seconds)
    • Enables HTTPS everywhere
    • Proves domain control only, not identity
    • Phishers get them too
    Best for: Almost every website
    👍 Situational
    OV

    Organization Validation

    • Organization named in the certificate
    • Paid; days to issue
    • Users never look
    Best for: Corporate policy requirements
    ⚠️ Legacy
    EV

    Extended Validation

    • Strictest identity checks
    • Expensive; browsers removed the green bar (~2019)
    • Research showed users didn’t notice
    Best for: Rarely worth it now
    ✔ section read

    13.8Let's Encrypt and ACME: certificates for everyone#

    Before 2015, certificates usually cost money and required manual paperwork, so many sites didn't bother with HTTPS. Let's Encrypt, a non-profit CA launched in 2015, changed that by offering free, fully automated DV certificates through the ACME protocol. Today it secures hundreds of millions of websites, and HTTPS is the default for the web.

    With Certbot (a popular ACME client), getting and installing a certificate on a typical web server is one command:

    Terminal
    # Get a certificate and configure nginx automatically
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com

# Test that automatic renewal works
sudo certbot renew --dry-run

    Other ACME tools: acme.sh, the Caddy web server (which gets certificates automatically with zero configuration), Traefik, and cert-manager for Kubernetes.

    ✔ section read

    13.9Why certificates expire, and why they're getting shorter#

    Certificate lifetimes keep shrinking:

    Period Maximum lifetime for public TLS certificates
    Early 2010s Up to 5 years
    2015 39 months (~3 years)
    2018 825 days (~2 years)
    September 2020 398 days (~13 months)
    March 2026 200 days
    March 2027 (planned) 100 days
    March 2029 (planned) 47 days

    (The last three steps come from a rule the CA/Browser Forum approved in 2025.) Let's Encrypt already issues 90-day certificates by default and has begun offering certificates that last only about six days.

    Why shorter?

    • Limits the damage if a private key is stolen or a certificate was issued by mistake: it stops working soon anyway.
    • Revocation is unreliable (next section), so short lifetimes are a more dependable safety net.
    • Forces automation, which eliminates the classic outage: "our certificate expired and nobody noticed."
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    13.10Revocation: cancelling a certificate early#

    If a server's private key is stolen, the certificate must be revoked before it expires. Several mechanisms exist, none perfect:

    Method How it works Problems
    CRL (Certificate Revocation List) The CA publishes a signed list of revoked serial numbers Lists can get large; clients must download them
    OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) The browser asks the CA: "Is serial #4aacbc… still good?" Slow; tells the CA which sites you visit; if the CA doesn't answer, browsers usually carry on anyway ("soft-fail"), which an attacker can exploit by blocking the request
    OCSP stapling The server fetches a fresh signed OCSP answer and attaches it to the handshake Better, but not universally deployed
    Browser-pushed lists The browser vendor collects revocations and pushes them to browsers (Chrome's CRLSets, Firefox's CRLite) Works well; this is where things are heading

    The industry is moving away from OCSP (Let's Encrypt shut down its OCSP service in 2025) toward CRLs, browser-pushed lists and very short certificate lifetimes.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Revocation methods

    👍 Situational
    CRL

    Signed list of revoked serials

    • Simple, offline-friendly
    • Making a comeback
    • Lists can get big
    • Clients must download them
    Best for: Browser-pushed lists & enterprise
    ⚠️ Legacy
    OCSP

    Ask the CA live

    • Fresh per-certificate status
    • Slow; leaks your browsing to the CA
    • Soft-fail lets attackers block it
    Best for: Being phased out (Let’s Encrypt ended it in 2025)
    👍 Situational
    OCSP stapling

    Server attaches the answer

    • No privacy leak; no extra round trip
    • Not universally deployed
    Best for: Servers that still use OCSP
    ✅ Use it
    Short-lived certs

    Expire before revocation matters

    • Damage window shrinks automatically
    • Forces automation
    • Requires reliable ACME automation
    Best for: The direction the industry is heading
    ✔ section read

    13.11Certificate Transparency: watching the watchers#

    Any trusted CA can technically issue a certificate for any domain. What if a CA is hacked or makes a mistake and issues a certificate for google.com to an attacker?

    Certificate Transparency (CT) makes every publicly trusted certificate public. CAs must submit certificates to several independent, append-only public logs (built as Merkle trees, Chapter 6). The log returns a signed receipt called an SCT (Signed Certificate Timestamp), which goes into the certificate. Chrome, Safari and Firefox reject publicly trusted certificates without valid SCTs.

    Domain owners can monitor the logs and get alerted if anyone ever issues a certificate for their domain.

    🧪 Try it yourself: search the logs for any domain at crt.sh, for example https://crt.sh/?q=example.com. You'll see every certificate ever issued for it.

    You can also tell CAs who is allowed to issue for your domain with a CAA DNS record:

    ✔ section read

    13.12Special kinds of certificates#

    Type What it's for
    Wildcard (*.example.com) Covers any single-level subdomain: www.example.com, api.example.com (but not a.b.example.com, and not example.com itself)
    Multi-domain (SAN) Lists several names in one certificate
    Self-signed Signs itself, with no CA. Fine for testing; browsers show a warning because nobody vouches for it.
    Private / internal CA A company runs its own CA for internal servers, devices and employees. Its root is installed only on company devices.
    Client certificate Identifies a user or device to a server (used in mutual TLS, Chapter 14)
    Code-signing certificate Signs software so operating systems can verify the publisher
    S/MIME certificate Signs and encrypts email (Chapter 16)
    Document-signing certificate Signs PDFs and legal documents
    ✔ section read

    13.13Certificate and key file formats#

    Certificate files come in confusingly many formats. Here's the decoder:

    Extension(s) Format Contains Typical use
    .pem, .crt, .cer PEM: Base64 text with -----BEGIN ...----- lines Certificates, keys, or both; can hold a chain Linux, nginx, Apache, most tools
    .der, .cer DER: raw binary One certificate or key Windows, Java, some devices
    .key Usually PEM A private key Server configuration
    .csr PEM A certificate signing request Sent to a CA
    .p12, .pfx PKCS#12: password-protected binary bundle Certificate + private key + chain Importing into Windows, macOS Keychain, browsers, Java
    .p7b, .p7c PKCS#7 Certificates only (no key) Windows chain bundles
    .jks Java KeyStore Keys and certificates Older Java applications

    Handy conversions:

    Terminal
    # PEM → DER, and back
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -outform DER -out cert.der
openssl x509 -in cert.der -inform DER -out cert.pem

# Bundle certificate + key + chain into a password-protected .p12/.pfx
openssl pkcs12 -export -in server.crt -inkey server.key \
  -certfile intermediate-ca.crt -out server.p12

# Extract certificate and key from a .p12
openssl pkcs12 -in server.p12 -nokeys -out cert.pem
openssl pkcs12 -in server.p12 -nocerts -nodes -out key.pem    # -nodes = leave key unencrypted

# Check that a certificate and private key belong together (the two outputs must match)
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl pkey -in server.key -pubout | openssl sha256
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Key and certificate file formats

    ✅ Use it
    PEM

    Base64 between BEGIN/END lines

    • Human-readable, copy-pasteable
    • Can hold a whole chain
    • Easy to confuse what’s inside
    Best for: Linux servers, nginx, OpenSSL
    👍 Situational
    DER

    Raw binary ASN.1

    • Compact; what’s actually signed
    • Not readable or pasteable
    Best for: Java, Windows, embedded
    👍 Situational
    PKCS#12 (.p12/.pfx)

    Password-protected bundle

    • Key + cert + chain in one file
    • Imports into Windows/macOS/Java
    • Old files use weak encryption
    • Password handling
    Best for: Moving identities between systems
    ✔ section read

    13.14When PKI goes wrong#

    📜 DigiNotar (2011). Hackers broke into DigiNotar, a Dutch CA, and issued over 500 fraudulent certificates, including one for *.google.com. It was used to intercept the Gmail traffic of an estimated 300,000 people in Iran. It was discovered because Chrome had Google's keys "pinned" (it knew what Google's certificates should look like). All browsers removed DigiNotar from their trust stores, and the company went bankrupt within weeks.

    📜 Symantec (2017–2018). After years of mis-issued certificates and poor oversight, Google and Mozilla gradually distrusted Symantec's CA business, one of the largest in the world at the time. Millions of websites had to replace their certificates.

    📜 Entrust (2024). After a long series of compliance failures, Chrome announced it would stop trusting new Entrust TLS certificates issued after late 2024. Other browsers followed.

    The lesson: the PKI system has a weakness, because any trusted CA can issue for any domain, and so it also has strong oversight. Certificate Transparency, CAA records, audits and browser root programs exist to catch and punish misbehavior.

    ✔ section read

    13.15Other ways to trust keys#

    Certificate authorities aren't the only approach:

    Model How it works Where it's used
    Hierarchical PKI (CAs) Trusted authorities vouch for keys The web, enterprise networks
    Trust on first use (TOFU) Trust the key the first time you see it; warn loudly if it ever changes SSH (Chapter 15)
    Web of trust Individuals sign each other's keys; you trust keys signed by people you trust PGP/GnuPG email
    Manual verification Compare fingerprints in person or over another channel Signal safety numbers
    DANE Publish the expected certificate in DNS, protected by DNSSEC Some email servers
    Pinning An app hard-codes the keys it expects for its own servers Mobile banking apps. (Pinning in browsers, "HPKP," was abandoned around 2018 because mistakes could lock a website out of its own users.)
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Ways to trust a key

    ✅ Use it
    Hierarchical PKI

    Certificate authorities

    • Scales to billions of users
    • Automatic for users
    • Any CA can issue for any domain (CT helps)
    • Central points of failure
    Best for: The web
    👍 Situational
    TOFU

    Trust on first use

    • Zero setup
    • Detects key changes later
    • The very first connection is unprotected
    Best for: SSH
    ⚠️ Legacy
    Web of trust

    People sign each other’s keys

    • No central authority
    • Hard to use; doesn’t scale
    • Leaks social graphs
    Best for: PGP enthusiasts
    ✅ Use it
    Manual fingerprints

    Compare out of band

    • Strongest assurance
    • Few people actually do it
    Best for: Signal safety numbers
    👍 Situational
    DANE

    Certificates in DNSSEC

    • Domain owner controls trust
    • Depends on DNSSEC deployment
    Best for: Mail servers
    👍 Situational
    Pinning

    App hard-codes expected keys

    • Blocks rogue CAs and interception
    • Mistakes lock users out (HPKP was abandoned)
    Best for: Mobile banking apps
    ✔ section read

    13.16🧪 Hands-on lab: build your own PKI#

    In this lab you'll act as a certificate authority. You'll create a root CA, an intermediate CA and a server certificate, then run an HTTPS server that trusts only your root. Every command was tested with OpenSSL 3.6. The lab uses elliptic-curve P-256 keys, a common choice for modern certificates.

    Terminal
    mkdir my-pki && cd my-pki

    Step 1: Create the root CA

    Terminal
    # The root's private key: the most precious file in your PKI
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out root-ca.key

# A self-signed root certificate, valid for 10 years
openssl req -x509 -new -key root-ca.key -sha256 -days 3650 \
  -subj "/C=US/O=My Learning Lab/CN=My Learning Root CA" \
  -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE" \
  -addext "keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign" \
  -out root-ca.crt

# Look at it: note that Issuer and Subject are the same (self-signed)
openssl x509 -in root-ca.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates

    Step 2: Create the intermediate CA

    Terminal
    # Intermediate key and CSR
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out intermediate-ca.key
openssl req -new -key intermediate-ca.key \
  -subj "/C=US/O=My Learning Lab/CN=My Learning Intermediate CA" \
  -out intermediate-ca.csr

# Rules for the intermediate: it IS a CA, but may not create further CAs (pathlen:0)
cat > intermediate-ext.cnf <<'EOF'
basicConstraints       = critical, CA:TRUE, pathlen:0
keyUsage               = critical, keyCertSign, cRLSign
subjectKeyIdentifier   = hash
authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always
EOF

# The ROOT signs the intermediate's CSR (valid 5 years)
openssl x509 -req -in intermediate-ca.csr \
  -CA root-ca.crt -CAkey root-ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -days 1825 -sha256 -extfile intermediate-ext.cnf \
  -out intermediate-ca.crt

    In a real CA, you would now lock root-ca.key away offline and use only the intermediate from here on.

    Step 3: Create a server key and CSR (what a website owner does)

    Terminal
    openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out server.key
openssl req -new -key server.key -subj "/CN=myapp.local" -out server.csr

# Inspect the CSR, and check its self-signature (proof the requester holds the private key)
openssl req -in server.csr -noout -text
openssl req -in server.csr -noout -verify
# Certificate request self-signature verify OK

    Step 4: The intermediate CA issues the server certificate

    Terminal
    # Rules for the server certificate: NOT a CA, used for TLS servers, valid for these names
cat > server-ext.cnf <<'EOF'
basicConstraints       = critical, CA:FALSE
keyUsage               = critical, digitalSignature
extendedKeyUsage       = serverAuth
subjectAltName         = DNS:myapp.local, DNS:localhost, IP:127.0.0.1
subjectKeyIdentifier   = hash
authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid
EOF

openssl x509 -req -in server.csr \
  -CA intermediate-ca.crt -CAkey intermediate-ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -days 90 -sha256 -extfile server-ext.cnf \
  -out server.crt

# The "full chain" file servers usually send: leaf first, then intermediate(s)
cat server.crt intermediate-ca.crt > server-fullchain.crt

    Step 5: Verify the chain of trust

    Terminal
    # Trust only our root; supply the intermediate as an "untrusted" helper
openssl verify -CAfile root-ca.crt -untrusted intermediate-ca.crt server.crt
# server.crt: OK

# What happens if the intermediate is missing? (The classic server misconfiguration)
openssl verify -CAfile root-ca.crt server.crt
# error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate

    Step 6: Inspect your certificate

    Terminal
    openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -text          # everything (compare with section 13.3)
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256

    Step 7: Run a real HTTPS server with your certificate

    In one terminal, start a test server:

    Terminal
    openssl s_server -accept 8443 -cert server.crt -key server.key \
  -cert_chain intermediate-ca.crt -www

    In a second terminal (in the same folder), connect to it:

    Terminal
    # curl, trusting only YOUR root CA
curl --cacert root-ca.crt https://localhost:8443/

# Or with OpenSSL's client, for a summary of the handshake
openssl s_client -connect localhost:8443 -servername localhost \
  -CAfile root-ca.crt -verify_return_error -brief </dev/null

    Output from s_client:

    You've just run a TLS 1.3 server with your own certificate chain, a post-quantum hybrid key exchange and AES-256-GCM encryption. Try curl https://localhost:8443/ without --cacert and you'll get a certificate error, because your system doesn't trust your root. That's exactly how a browser reacts to an unknown CA. Press Ctrl+C in the first terminal to stop the server.

    Step 8 (optional): Client certificates for mutual TLS

    Terminal
    cat > client-ext.cnf <<'EOF'
basicConstraints       = critical, CA:FALSE
keyUsage               = critical, digitalSignature
extendedKeyUsage       = clientAuth
EOF

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out client.key
openssl req -new -key client.key -subj "/CN=alice" -out client.csr
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA intermediate-ca.crt -CAkey intermediate-ca.key \
  -CAcreateserial -days 30 -sha256 -extfile client-ext.cnf -out client.crt
cat client.crt intermediate-ca.crt > client-chain.crt

# Server that REQUIRES a client certificate from our PKI
openssl s_server -accept 8444 -cert server.crt -key server.key \
  -cert_chain intermediate-ca.crt -CAfile root-ca.crt -chainCAfile intermediate-ca.crt \
  -Verify 1 -verify_return_error -www

    In the second terminal:

    Terminal
    curl --cacert root-ca.crt https://localhost:8444/                    # rejected: no client cert
curl --cacert root-ca.crt --cert client-chain.crt --key client.key \
  https://localhost:8444/                                            # accepted

    Step 9 (optional): Package for other systems

    Terminal
    # A .p12 bundle for importing into Windows, macOS Keychain or Java
openssl pkcs12 -export -in server.crt -inkey server.key \
  -certfile intermediate-ca.crt -out server.p12

    Step 10 (optional, be careful): Make your computer trust your root

    ⚠️ Watch out: whoever holds a trusted root's private key can impersonate any website to your computer. Only do this on a test machine, keep root-ca.key safe, and remove the root when you're done. For local development, the tool mkcert automates all of this safely.

    Terminal
    # macOS
sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
  -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain root-ca.crt

# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo cp root-ca.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/my-learning-root.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates

    On Windows, double-click root-ca.crt → Install Certificate → Local Machine → Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

    Bonus: inspect a real website's certificates

    Terminal
    # Show the certificate chain a site sends
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null

# Just the essentials: who it's for, who issued it, when it expires
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
